abase

/uh-BAYS/ - rhymes with place · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Abase means to lower someone's dignity on purpose — pushing a person down in their own eyes or the world's.

The debtors' court of that era recovered little money; its real business was to abase borrowers, who stood in the square wearing placards that itemized what they owed.

Example

When the debate club's president lost a wager, the winners demanded he read his worst freshman essay aloud at the annual dinner; the club later retired the tradition, agreeing that a game meant to tease had begun to abase its losers instead.

Abase is stronger than embarrass: an embarrassment fades with the blush, but to abase someone is to push their dignity down on purpose — the word always involves lowering a person, in their own eyes or the world's.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

degrade: To degrade is to lower worth or condition, often gradually — a reputation, a road surface, even a signal can degrade over time. To abase is sharper and personal: one person's dignity deliberately pushed down, usually in public. Degradation can happen by neglect; abasement is engineered.

demean: To demean someone is to treat or speak to them as less than they are — a demeaning chore, a demeaning tone. Abase goes further and more publicly: it strips a person's standing on purpose, lowering them in their own eyes or the world's.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

dignify: to lend someone standing and respect

ennoble: to raise a person up, morally or socially

Where it sits · how far the person is dragged down

embarrass → humiliate → abase

embarrass vs. abase: To embarrass someone is far milder than to abase them — a blush passes, and no one's dignity is really taken.

humiliate vs. abase: Humiliate stops just short of abase: both shame a person publicly, but abase adds the sense of grinding someone down to a lower station.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — a-: to, toward (from Latin ad-)

Root — base: low (from Late Latin bassus)

Put it together: A- (to, toward) + base (low) = to bring someone toward the low. English took Old French abaissier, 'to lower,' built on bassus, low — the same 'low' you hear in the base of a mountain and in a base act, a deed as low as conduct gets.

Use the root in a new word: basement: The flood turned the basement — the house's lowest level — into a shallow pond by morning.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Abase is a heavy, formal word for deliberately lowering someone's dignity. For everyday wounds, humiliate or embarrass will do; save abase for public, engineered degradation. Keep its unit neighbors straight: upbraid scolds someone for a fault, and vituperate buries them in abusive words — abase strips status rather than delivering a lecture.
